question: What is the very first step when you want to start a nursing research project?
explanation: Every good study starts by figuring out what the exact problem is. You have to spot the gap in patient care before you can start gathering any data!

question: Why do we need to clearly identify our research problem before jumping into the study?

options.A: It guarantees the hospital will approve the project
options.B: It gives the entire study clear direction and focus
options.C: It prevents patients from asking questions
options.D: It removes the need for a literature review

explanation: Think of the problem statement as your map. When you know exactly what you are looking into, you won't wander around aimlessly while trying to collect your data.

question: Which of these is NOT something a good nursing research problem should be?

options.B: It must cause physical harm to test resilience
options.C: It must be significant to patient care
options.D: It must be ethical to study

explanation: Never! As nurses, our golden rule is 'do no harm.' Ethical research will never intentionally cause physical or emotional pain to patients.

question: What does it mean when we say a nursing research problem must be empirically testable?

options.A: It requires no data collection from patients
options.B: It only relies on personal opinions and feelings
options.C: It has already been solved in past decades
options.D: The variables can be observed and measured

explanation: Empirical just means we can actually see, count, or measure it in the real world rather than just guessing or going purely on vibes!

question: Where do bedside nurses usually get the best ideas for a research topic?

options.D: Daily clinical observations and ward routines

explanation: Your time on the ward is a goldmine! Noticing what gives patients trouble during your daily shift is the number one way to find real research topics.

question: How does reading professional nursing journals help you find a great research topic?

options.A: It points out existing knowledge gaps and areas needing more study
options.B: It gives exact answers for every single patient diagnosis
options.C: It eliminates the need to ever talk to patients
options.D: It automatically provides funding for hospital equipment

explanation: When you read past studies, the authors usually drop hints at the end about what they didn't get to figure out. That's your cue to step in!

question: What is the biggest risk if you start a research project with a topic that is too vague or broad?

options.A: The hospital administration will immediately ban the study
options.B: The study becomes too messy and hard to manage
options.C: Patients will refuse to take their medications
options.D: It guarantees the results will be published internationally

explanation: If your topic is too wide, you'll end up with mountains of random data that don't make sense. Narrowing it down keeps your project neat and stress-free.

question: A nurse notices that new mothers in the postnatal ward look anxious about breastfeeding. Which option turns this into a well-focused research study?

options.A: Asking every nurse on the ward how they feel about their personal jobs
options.B: Reviewing the financial cost of building a new maternity ward
options.C: Studying why the entire healthcare system in the country is failing mothers
options.D: Evaluating whether a peer support group lowers anxiety scores among first-time breastfeeding mothers

explanation: Spot on! This takes a real ward observation (breastfeeding anxiety) and turns it into a clear, measurable plan with a specific group of people.

question: What is the main job of a problem statement in your research proposal?

options.A: To provide a summary of the statistical results
options.B: To explain the background and why the issue needs attention
options.C: To offer final medical advice to patients
options.D: To list the personal biographies of the researchers

explanation: The problem statement tells your reader: 'Here is what is going wrong, here is why it matters, and here is why we need to fix it right now.'

question: How is a purpose statement different from a problem statement?

options.A: The problem statement contains all the final conclusions
options.B: The problem statement is written after data is collected
options.C: The purpose statement only lists financial costs
options.D: The purpose statement declares the direct aim or goal of the study

explanation: While the problem statement highlights the trouble or gap, the purpose statement tells us what your study specifically plans to do about it.

question: Which of these is a feasibility constraint you must think about when choosing a research topic?

options.A: The personal fashion style of the lead researcher
options.B: The historical century when nursing began
options.D: The color scheme of the hospital walls

explanation: Feasibility just means asking yourself: 'Do I have enough time, money, and resources to actually pull this off without crashing?'

question: A student wants to study post-operative pain across fifty hospitals nationwide in just two weeks with zero funding. What is the major flaw here?

options.A: Patients do not experience pain after surgery
options.B: The topic is completely unrelated to nursing care
options.C: Hospital staff never want to improve pain management
options.D: The study lacks practical feasibility due to time and budget limits

explanation: We would all love to save the world in two weeks for free, but it's simply not realistic! Always make sure your study matches your actual time and pockets.

question: Why do researchers need to narrow down a massive topic like 'hospital stress'?

options.A: Broad topics are too massive and vague to study effectively all at once
options.B: Patients refuse to talk about general topics
options.C: Narrowing a topic increases the financial cost of the study
options.D: Broad topics are illegal to research in clinical settings

explanation: If your topic is as big as the ocean, you'll drown in data! Narrowing it down gives you a specific pool you can easily swim across.

question: What is the happy result of successfully narrowing down your nursing research topic?

options.A: The complete elimination of all hospital illnesses
options.B: A specific, manageable question that can be investigated thoroughly
options.C: A massive textbook that covers every disease in medicine
options.D: An automatic guarantee of winning a research award

explanation: When you narrow your focus, you end up with a sharp, clear question that you can actually research, answer, and feel proud of!
